newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: RALLY TODAY OUTSIDE BURMA'S EMBASSY
A rally today in Canberra by Australia's Burmese community, will call on the Australian Government to take action to help return democratic government to Burma.

Protesters at the rally outside Burma's embassy, are expected to denounce Burma's State Law and Order Restoration Council, or SLORC, and call for economic and political sanctions against the country's military regime.
Group spokesman, Maung Maung Than says the Burmese community in Australia was heartened by support last week from the Federal Opposition for the imposition of sanctions.
Mr Than says the move now has the support of the ALP, Greens and Democrats.
CALL FOR INQUIRY FOLLOWING TV-TOWER STUDY
Federal Science Technology Minister Peter McGauran has called for an urgent inquiry into possible links between childhood leukaemia and radiation from telephone and television towers.
That follows the release yesterday of an 18-year study of children living near three tv-towers in Sydney.
The study, by four-researchers from Melbourne, found a higher incidence of leukaemia among those children compared to others living away from the towers.
Standards Australia is due to vote shortly on whether to allow a five-fold increase in radiation limits for phone and tv towers, but Mr McGauran wants it to delay any vote.
WA ELECTION CAMPAIGN ENTERS LAST WEEK
West Australian Premier Richard Court and Labor leader Geoff Gallop both head south today as the election campaign enters its last week.
Mr Court moves into presidential campaign style today, travelling by bus from Bunbury to Geraldton.
He plans to visit all of Liberal marginal seats and stop off in Mandurah for a visit to his father, Sir Charles Court.
Dr Gallop travels to Kwinana this morning where he'll launch Labor's industrial relations policy.
SUPPORT FOR NATIONAL EAST-WEST HIGHWAY
There's further support for a national highway running east-west through the centre of Australia.
The Australian Local Government Association Congress has called on the Federal Government to extend the national highway network to include strategic road links across the interior of Australia.
The motion was put forward by the Laverton Shire Council, which along with other groups, has had talks with Federal Transport and Regional Development Minister, John Sharp.
Transport ministers from Western Australia, the Northern Territory and Queensland have already shown their support by forming a working party.
A number of councils in the three States have also given their approval.
US ATTACKS AUSTRALIA OVER CHILD LABOUR ISSUE AT WTO
The U-S ambassador at the first ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation in Singapore, has attacked Australia's position not to support a push to discuss child labour and human rights.
The U-S is leading the move to have the issues included for discussion at this week's meeting, where 125 countries will discuss and formulate the rules that will govern world buisness.
The developing nations, spearheaded by south-east Asian countries, are against the idea and they're being supported by Australia.
Trade Minister Tim Fisher, who's in Singapore, has defended Australia's position.
But U-S Ambassador Andrew Stoller, says Australia's position is a major disappointment, and could damage its attempts at home to push for further tariff reductions.
AUSTRALIAN BAT VIRUS CLOSE TO AMERICAN RABIES
An American scientist says he's surprised how close the new strain of lyssa virus, found in Australian bats, is to the American rabies virus.
American and Australian scientists will meet this week to consider joint research into the lyssa virus.
The U-S Centre for Disease Control has been studying the lyssa virus, and wants to help Australian researchers find out how widespread and contagious it is.
The C-D-C's chief of rabies research, Doctor Charles Rupprecht, who helped identify the new virus, says the new strain of lyssa virus is as close to rabies as it gets.
AMA TO RECONSIDER DOCTORS STRIKE
The Australian Medical Association will reconsider a national doctors strike planned for Wednesday if the Federal Government considers amendments to its plan to reduce G-P numbers.
The Coalition wants all aspiring GP's to do four years post-graduate training before they're eligible for a Medicare
Provider Number which will only be given to 400 graduates.
The A-M-A's says it's willing to suspend the strike if the Government agrees to proposed Democrat amendments minimising the impact of the crack-down on current medical students.
Health Minister Michael Wooldridge will hold further talks with the Democrats before the budget measure comes up for a vote in the Senate.
PRO-GUN CAMPAIGN "INSULT TO PORT ARTHUR VICTIMS' FAMILIES"
The Tasmanian Coalition for Gun Control has described a national campaign by the shooters' lobby against gun laws as an insult to families of the Port Arthur victims.
The Sporting Shooters Association will spend one million dollars on the campaign, much of the budget spent on television advertising.
Roland Browne, the co-ordinator of the Tasmanian Coalition for Gun Control, says the campaign is ill-timed and that the million dollars should go to the Port Arthur Trust Fund.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
